source.title: Tackling Noisy Labels With Network Parameter Additive Decomposition
source.authors: Jingyi Wang; Xiao-Bo Xia; Long Lan; Xinghao Wu; Jun Yu; Wen-Jing Yang; Bo Han; Tong-Liang Liu

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, though some tables are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies training on noisy labels and reports test accuracy across noise conditions, but does not measure the original claim’s training-error, random-label, optimization-time, unstructured-input, regularization-removal, or learning-order outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy under simulated label noise and real-world noisy labels. It does not report training error on noisy labels. Results it attributes to prior work, including the general memorization-order claim, are not extracted as results of this study. Table 2’s supplied flattened text does not reliably preserve every dataset, method, and condition association; Table 5’s layout supports extraction of its Standard rows for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
record.test_reason: The study uses the memorization effect to design a noisy-label mitigation method and reports generalization performance. It does not measure training-set memorization, fitting completely random labels, or the order of learning clean and mislabeled examples. Its Standard baseline uses validation-based early stopping, so declining test accuracy across noise rates does not establish V4's degradation while perfectly fitting the training set.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate as a statement of the authors' proposed mechanism: additive parameter decomposition with dynamic constraints improves noisy-label robustness by assigning clean-data learning and mislabeled-data effects to different parameter groups. The experiments demonstrate classification-performance improvements, rather than directly verifying that the groups separately memorize clean and mislabeled examples.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes additive parameter decomposition with time-varying parameter constraints, evaluated on simulated and real-world noisy-label datasets; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that results vary with the noise rate and with the chosen β2 function and its hyperparameter c2.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard test accuracy decreases across 60%, 70%, and 80% symmetric noise: 78.33, 71.62, and 48.89% on CIFAR-10; 48.62, 38.12, and 21.15% on CIFAR-100. Training-set fit is unreported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With validation-based early stopping, standard classifiers generalize less accurately as symmetric label noise increases across these tested rates.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The paper does not report training accuracy or training error for the noisy-label experiments. Table 2’s supplied flattened text does not reliably preserve all row and condition associations. Food-101 and Clothing1M results use one experiment; Table 5 reports five trials.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2’s simulated-noise test-accuracy values were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve all dataset, method, and condition associations. Tables 3, 4, 6, and 7 report noisy-label classification performance or method comparisons but do not add a distinct measurement of the V4 training-fit outcome.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Training-set fitting with shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and test degradation while retaining that fit. Reported test accuracies cover selected noise rates without training-error measurements or the fully random endpoint.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms true-label generalization.

Direct comparison of clean-label and noisy-label learning over training. The learning order is adopted from prior work; test-accuracy trajectories and test-feature visualizations do not measure that order.

record.verdict_notes: Table 5's CIFAR-100 entries are arranged by noise-rate columns, with methods running down each column. The extraction mistakenly treated three consecutive entries in the 80% column as Standard results across three noise rates.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training experiment or training-error result.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed for random versus true labels.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

The study reports test accuracy at different symmetric label-noise rates, but does not report training-set fit, perfect training accuracy, or whether the network captures remaining signal while memorizing noise. The relevant Table 2 values cannot be assigned reliably from the supplied flattened text; Table 5’s relevant Standard rows are extracted.
No experiment removes weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation to test random-label fitting or generalization.
The paper describes memorization order in its abstract and discussion of prior work, but does not itself measure whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy-label patterns.

rows.size_stated: CIFAR-10; network architecture not stated in Table 5
rows.operation_detail: Train with cross-entropy on simulated symmetric label noise; report test accuracy.
rows.note: Test accuracy alone does not establish the version’s training-fit requirement.
rows.check: The value is correctly transcribed, but measures test accuracy rather than memorization or degradation conditional on perfect training fit. Section 4.1 identifies the CIFAR-10 architecture as ResNet-18; Standard uses validation-based early stopping.
